issues.legal_issue: A final order in a proceeding concerning possession need not repeat a finding that a breach of the peace exists when the preliminary order recorded the Magistrate’s reasons for that satisfaction and the dispute has not been shown to have ceased.
material_facts: The Magistrate’s preliminary order recorded reasons for being satisfied that a breach of the peace existed.
The parties took contradictory positions about whether there was an apprehension of a breach of the peace, and neither asserted that the dispute had ceased.
After a full enquiry into possession, the Magistrate made a final order without repeating a finding about the breach of the peace.
issues.conclusion: The omission to make a fresh finding about a breach of the peace in the final order did not invalidate it; absent clear evidence that the dispute had ceased, the proceedings could continue to a final order.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 145(1), 145(4), 145(5), and 145(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, once the Magistrate records the required satisfaction in the preliminary order, the enquiry proceeds to determine actual possession and need not include a fresh finding at every stage that a breach of the peace exists. Proceedings may be stopped under Section 145(5) if the dispute is shown to have ceased. R. H. Bhutani v. Miss Mani J. Desai, Hari Ram v. Banwari Lal, and Ramarao v. Shivram support these principles. The High Court in revision cannot reweigh the sufficiency of the material underlying the Magistrate’s satisfaction.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a finding about a breach of the peace in a final order is not, in the circumstances, a manifest defect warranting interference under the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction.
material_facts: The preliminary order recorded the Magistrate’s satisfaction that a breach of the peace existed.
The final order omitted a separate finding on that issue, but the parties’ contradictory positions did not show that the dispute had ceased.
The respondents sought to have the Magistrate’s order quashed under the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The omission was not a manifest defect that justified quashing the final order under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not warrant interference merely because a final order omits a repeated finding about a breach of the peace where the preliminary order recorded the Magistrate’s satisfaction and the circumstances do not show that the dispute ceased. R. H. Bhutani v. Miss Mani J. Desai supports the rule that the required satisfaction is recorded before the enquiry and need not persist as a separate finding at the final stage.

issues.legal_issue: An omission to mention a breach of the peace in a final order is a curable procedural irregularity that does not vitiate the order when the parties had a full opportunity to present evidence and suffered no prejudice.
material_facts: The Magistrate’s final order omitted a statement that a breach of the peace existed.
Both parties had the full opportunity to produce evidence before the Magistrate.
The record did not show that either party suffered prejudice from the omission.
issues.conclusion: The omission was, at most, a curable procedural irregularity and did not vitiate the Magistrate’s order.
issues.legal_principle: A procedural error that causes no prejudice and does not impair the parties’ opportunity to present evidence is a curable irregularity and is not sufficient to vitiate an order. This principle was applied to the omission in a proceeding under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
